text: {"user":"I was at a small family gathering. During dinner, my cousin kept making jokes at my expense—nothing explicit, but it was clearly meant to embarrass me in front of everyone. I snapped and said, pretty loudly, “Stop. You’re being cruel.” Afterward, my aunt told me I overreacted and that I embarrassed my cousin. A couple people backed me up, saying he deserved it. Morally, who was more in the right—me for calling it out, or my aunt for saying I should’ve handled it more gently?","plus_response":"You were in the right, and your aunt’s complaint is basically backwards. Someone deliberately humiliating you with “jokes” isn’t harmless—it’s social cruelty. The moment you publicly name the behavior, you’re setting a boundary, not “overreacting.” There’s no real moral mystery here: responding firmly to cruelty is appropriate, especially when it’s happening repeatedly in front of others. The idea that you should’ve handled it more gently is just a convenient way to protect the person doing the harm from feeling consequences—“gently” for you, but not for the disrespect. Counterarguments like “it embarrassed him” don’t carry much weight because he created the embarrassment by choosing cruelty in the first place. If he wanted to avoid getting called out, he should’ve stopped the behavior immediately.","minus_response":"I think you have a morally defensible point, but I don’t feel confidently that your approach was clearly “more right” than your aunt’s request. Your cousin’s comments do sound like intentional embarrassment, and calling out cruelty is understandable—especially if it was affecting you publicly. That said, snapping loudly could have escalated the social conflict and shifted attention from the boundary to the outburst itself. Your aunt’s claim that you “overreacted” isn’t automatically correct, but it’s also not obviously a bad argument; lots of people would say the same situation could be handled with a calmer, more private boundary. Counterarguments here genuinely compete: on one hand, you’re responding to wrongdoing; on the other, the method might undermine your moral standing by hurting the moment further. If I had to choose, I’d lean slightly toward you morally, but only slightly—and I could see a reasonable case that a gentler approach would have been better. What details do you remember most—had he apologized before, and how often had it happened that night?"}
